dimensions.name: Requirements clarification
dimensions.description: Clarifies ledger scope, money movement types, settlement, audit, and consistency expectations.

levels.1: Restates the prompt without defining double-entry bookkeeping or idempotency.
levels.2: Lists payments and refunds but omits settlement, reconciliation, or audit retention.
levels.3: Separates functional and non-functional requirements and states assumptions about providers, currencies, and corrections.
levels.4: Also prioritizes requirements, defines the durability and audit boundaries, and connects regulatory or reconciliation needs to design constraints.

dimensions.name: Back-of-envelope estimation
dimensions.description: Derives write/read QPS, storage for postings and audit data, and reconciliation burst load.

levels.1: Repeats the numbers without deriving capacity.
levels.2: Computes average QPS but ignores postings per transfer, storage, or month-end bursts.
levels.3: Estimates average and peak write/read rates and the storage needed for postings and retained audit data.
levels.4: Also estimates index size, replica lag tolerance, reconciliation throughput, and headroom for payout windows.

dimensions.name: API and data model
dimensions.description: Defines transfer/refund APIs with idempotency and a double-entry posting model.

levels.1: No clear API or accounting model.
levels.2: Has payment endpoints but no balanced postings or idempotency contract.
levels.3: Defines request/response shapes, idempotency keys, accounts, entries, and postings with a balance invariant.
levels.4: Also explains append-only corrections, deferred constraints, request-hash mismatch handling, and how balances are derived or verified.

dimensions.name: High-level architecture
dimensions.description: Separates the ledger transaction, settlement, outbox, and reconciliation.

levels.1: A single service that writes balances directly.
levels.2: Names components but does not show how a transfer reaches settlement.
levels.3: Shows the transactional ledger path, outbox, settlement workers, and reconciliation jobs.
levels.4: Also explains why provider calls stay outside the transaction, how retries traverse each boundary, and how read replicas are used safely.

dimensions.name: Deep dives
dimensions.description: Explains commit, settlement, and reconciliation with concrete failure handling.

levels.1: No deep dive beyond the API.
levels.2: Covers commit or settlement but leaves reconciliation and retries vague.
levels.3: Covers the atomic commit, idempotent settlement, and statement reconciliation with implementable detail.
levels.4: Also handles ambiguous timeouts, duplicate provider charges, compensating entries, invariant checks, and audit preservation.

dimensions.name: Trade-offs
dimensions.description: Compares consistency, sharding, settlement timing, and correction strategies.

levels.2: Names one trade-off without connecting it to the ledger design.
levels.3: Compares meaningful choices such as append-only vs mutable balances, or synchronous vs asynchronous settlement.
levels.4: Also explains when the chosen approach breaks down and how the team would detect and revisit it.

dimensions.name: Communication and failure handling
dimensions.description: Presents the design and invariants clearly, with audit, monitoring, and recovery.

levels.1: Disorganized and assumes money movement cannot fail.
levels.2: Understandable but omits several failure or audit paths.
levels.3: Explains the flow clearly and covers duplicate requests, provider outages, reconciliation, and monitoring.
levels.4: Also covers balance-check failures, locked periods, regulatory audit access, and a concise summary of the invariants that must never break.
